statement: In statistics, a linear model estimates the relationship between a scalar response (dependent variable) $y_i$ and one or more explanatory variables $\vec{x_i} = [x_1^i, x_2^i, \ldots, x_m^i]$ via a linear combination of unknown parameters $\vec{\beta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_m]$: $y_i \approx \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^m \beta_j x_j^i$. When $\vec{x_i}$ is extended to include an intercept $[1, x_1^i, \ldots, x_m^i]$, the model prediction is the dot product $y_i \approx \vec{\beta} \cdot \vec{x_i}$, or in matrix form for a dataset, $Y \approx X\vec{\beta}$.

symbols.meaning: scalar response or dependent variable for observation $i$
vector of explanatory variables (extended with 1 for the intercept: $[1, x_1^i, \dots, x_m^i]$)
design matrix of independent variables / predictors

properties.property: A linear model with exactly one explanatory variable is a simple linear regression, whereas a model with two or more explanatory variables is a multiple linear regression.
properties.why: classification based on the number of predictor variables

properties.property: Linear regression focuses on the conditional probability distribution of the response given the predictors (most commonly modeling the conditional mean as an affine function) rather than the joint distribution.
properties.why: characterizes the regression relationship as conditional on predictors

properties.property: Under least-squares estimation minimizing $L(D, \vec{\beta}) = \|X\vec{\beta} - Y\|^2$, the optimal parameter estimate satisfies $X^{\textsf{T}}X\vec{\beta} = X^{\textsf{T}}Y$, which yields $\vec{\hat{\beta}} = (X^{\textsf{T}}X)^{-1}X^{\textsf{T}}Y$ when $X^{\textsf{T}}X$ is invertible.
properties.why: setting the gradient of the convex squared-error loss function to zero yields the normal equations

properties.property: Under Gaussian distributed responses with mean $\vec{\beta} \cdot \vec{x_i}$ and fixed variance $\sigma^2$, maximum likelihood estimation yields the identical parameter estimate to ordinary least squares.
properties.why: maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood function is equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared residuals

assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation (or relationship) of the response given the predictors is an affine function of the predictors: $\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid \vec{x_i}] = \vec{\beta} \cdot \vec{x_i}$.
assumptions.breaks_when: The true relationship between the predictors and the response is non-linear.

assumptions.assumption: The matrix $X^{\textsf{T}}X$ is non-singular and invertible.
assumptions.breaks_when: Predictors are linearly dependent (perfect multicollinearity) or there are more covariates than observations ($m > n$).

assumptions.assumption: For MLE equivalence with OLS, the observations $y_i$ are conditionally independent normal random variables with constant variance $\sigma^2$.
assumptions.breaks_when: Errors exhibit heavy-tailed distributions, Laplace distributions, heteroscedasticity, or correlation.

failure_modes.mode: Singular or non-invertible design matrix cross-product
failure_modes.signature: $X^{\textsf{T}}X$ cannot be inverted, preventing direct closed-form computation of $\vec{\hat{\beta}} = (X^{\textsf{T}}X)^{-1}X^{\textsf{T}}Y$.
failure_modes.cause: Exact multicollinearity among explanatory variables or high-dimensional covariate vectors where $m \ge n$.

failure_modes.mode: Sensitivity to outliers under least squares
failure_modes.signature: Parameter estimates $\vec{\hat{\beta}}$ are substantially distorted by a small number of extreme observations.
failure_modes.cause: Least squares uses a quadratic penalty $(y_i - \vec{\beta} \cdot \vec{x_i})^2$ which disproportionately weights large residuals in the presence of heavy-tailed error distributions.
